metaDescription: Six corded hand blenders at or under $50, compared on real motor power, blade guards, speed control and attachment sets, with honest limits for each.
expertTake: The Braun MultiQuick 5 is the best pick at this level because its bell-shaped shaft cuts splatter and its motor is built by a company that sells these as its main business. The KOIOS 1000W anti-scratch model is the value pick if you want a kit. If you only puree soup twice a year, a simple 400W stick is all you need.
introParagraphs: An immersion blender is a motor handle with a long shaft and a bladed foot that you lower into the pot. It saves washing a jug and moves nothing but the food in front of the blade, so it suits soup, sauce, smoothies and baby food.

Prices move, and the $50 cap in this guide reflects listing prices when it was last updated. At this tier the headline wattage is mostly marketing, so the shape of the blade guard, the speed control and the build matter more than the number on the box.

products.name: Braun MultiQuick 5 Hand Blender, 350W, Beaker and Whisk
products.description:
Braun builds this around the shaft. The bell-shaped foot is designed to reduce suction, which stops the blade from gripping the pot bottom, and the blade sits inside the bell so splatter is contained. The stainless steel blades are hardened for chopping, and a beaker and whisk come in the box.

At 350 watts it has less rated power than the 1000W models below, but rated watts are a loose guide. Blade shape, bell geometry and motor quality decide how well it blends soup, and Braun's reputation rests on that. It offers two speeds, which is fewer steps than the 12-speed KOIOS but easier to use.

In ownership the bell shaft detaches for washing, and the motor is the part that ages. Do not run it dry or in a nonstick pot without care. It sits in the upper-middle price tier of the group, a fair premium for a tool you will use for years.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a reliable soup and sauce blender with minimal mess.
pros: Bell-shaped shaft reduces suction and splatter
cons: 350W is the lowest rated power of the group

products.name: KOIOS 1000W Anti-Scratch 3-in-1 Immersion Blender
products.description:
KOIOS gives you the largest number on the box at the second-lowest price tier. A 1000 watt rating, 12 speeds and a four-tip 304 stainless blade are paired with an anti-scratch guard meant to protect nonstick cookware.

Peak wattage and continuous wattage are different, so treat the 1000W figure as a burst rating, not a promise of heavy-duty torque. The anti-scratch guard is the real value, because a bare blade will scrape a nonstick pot. Next to the 350W Braun it has about three times the headline power, but the bell shaft and splatter control are simpler.

Expect a plastic body that is comfortable but not premium. Clean it by running the shaft in warm soapy water straight after use, and do not submerge the motor. It is a solid kit for someone who wants variable control.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want variable speed and a kit at a low price.
cons: Less splatter control than the Braun

products.name: KOIOS 5-in-1 Immersion Blender, 1000W, 12 Speeds, Turbo
products.description:
This KOIOS is the kit version. A blender stick, chopper, whisk, frother and beaker replace several small appliances, and 12 speeds plus a turbo button cover soft to very smooth. The 304 stainless shaft is designed to fit pots, mason jars and wide-mouth cups.

The chopper and whisk are the useful extras. They turn the stick into a mini processor for herbs and a hand mixer for cream, which is helpful in a small kitchen. Compared with the 3-in-1 KOIOS it adds the frother and chopper and sits slightly higher in the price tiers.

Store the attachments in a drawer organizer so none are lost. The same warnings apply: do not run the chopper empty, and let hot soup cool a little before blending. For a first immersion blender it is a convenient bundle.
products.bestFor: First-time buyers who want a stick, chopper, whisk and frother in one box.
pros: Turbo button on top of 12 speeds

products.name: Turelar 1100W 5-in-1 Corded Immersion Blender, Trigger Speed
products.description:
Turelar chooses a trigger instead of buttons. Press harder for more speed, which gives a continuous range in one hand, and the nylon blade guard reduces suction and protects pots. The maker lists a full copper motor at 1100 watts.

A pressure trigger feels natural once you have used it, because you can feather the speed while blending a hot soup. It is also easy to overdo, so start gently or the contents will spray. In headline power it tops the group, and it sits in the middle price tier.

The kit adds the usual attachments. Wash the nylon guard after use because food collects under it. If you like intuitive control, this is a good fit.
products.bestFor: Cooks who prefer pressure-sensitive speed control with one hand.
pros: Nylon guard reduces suction and scratching
Highest listed wattage of the group

products.name: Bonsenkitchen 4-in-1 Immersion Blender, 500W, 12 Speeds
products.description:
Bonsenkitchen pairs a 500 watt high-torque motor with a food processor attachment. Twelve speeds and a turbo mode cover the range, and a scratch-resistant stainless body is splash-resistant.

Its 500W rating is lower than the 1000W KOIOS pair but is stated as a high-torque figure, and honest ratings in the middle of the range often feel stronger than headline peaks. The processor bowl handles onions and nuts, which the stick alone cannot. It sits at the middle-upper price tier here.

Keep the processor lid dry and wash blades carefully. It suits a small kitchen without a countertop food processor. Expect the bowl to handle a cup or two of onions or nuts at a time, so large batches of salsa mean working in rounds. The motor head needs a pause between rounds, as with any compact motor that is asked to chop for several minutes.
products.bestFor: Small kitchens that want a mini processor bowl with the stick.

products.name: MasterChef 400W Stainless Immersion Blender
products.description:
MasterChef is the plain choice. A 400 watt motor, a stainless blending shaft and simple controls handle soups and smoothies. The brand name is licensed, so it does not tell you who built the motor.

With 400 watts it ranks in the middle of the wattage range here, above the Braun's 350W. It lacks the variable control of the KOIOS or Turelar, so you get on and off. The price tier is the third cheapest of the six.

It is fine for occasional soup. Clean the shaft right after use and avoid dry running. Because the controls are basic, tilt the pot slightly and move the foot in slow circles to draw food into the blade, since there is no low speed to tame a splash. It will not replace a stronger tool for thick hummus or nut butters, which stall a 400W motor.
products.bestFor: Occasional users who want the simplest and cheapest option.
pros: Lower price tier in the group
cons: Licensed brand name tells you little about the motor

buyingCriteria.explanation: Watt ratings at this price are usually peak burst figures. The Braun at 350W can out-blend a 1000W stick if its bell shaft and blade geometry are better. Judge by shape, build and speed range, not by the largest number. A useful sanity check is to see whether the maker publishes continuous operating time, since a stick that must rest after one minute is telling you its true duty cycle. Most hand blenders are rated for short bursts of a minute or two before a cooldown.
A bare steel blade scrapes nonstick pots. The KOIOS anti-scratch model and Turelar nylon guard address this. Always blend in a pot with the heat off.

The KOIOS pair gives 12 speeds on a dial, the Turelar uses a pressure trigger and the Braun has two speeds. Variable control matters for hot soup, where full speed sprays. Start low and ramp up. Many cooks never use more than the bottom third of the range, so a stick with a gentle low end is more useful than one with a fierce top end. If you plan to make mayonnaise, the slowest setting with the blade resting on the jar bottom produces the best emulsion.
Choppers, whisks and beakers add value only if you use them. The KOIOS 5-in-1 and Bonsenkitchen bring a chopper or processor, while the MasterChef is blender only. Count the tools you already own.

A shaft of about 8 or 9 inches reaches the bottom of a deep stockpot. Short shafts leave you tilting the pot. Check that the blending foot fits your widest jar. A foot around two inches across passes into most mason jars and narrow cups, while a wider bell needs a bigger container. Also check that the shaft is long enough to stay submerged without the motor housing touching liquid.

All of these are corded, so cord length and outlet position affect where you cook. Cordless is rare at this tier. Wipe the handle clean of grease. Longer sessions, such as batch soup, tire the wrist, so a grip that stays comfortable with wet hands is worth checking. A lighter motor head helps, though it often means a smaller motor.

specDecoder.meaning: A brief burst figure at the motor, not what it holds under thick loads.
specDecoder.watchFor: The KOIOS pair and Turelar quote peak numbers; the Braun lists 350W.

specDecoder.meaning: Steps between the lowest and highest motor speed.
specDecoder.watchFor: Useful only if the low steps are slow enough for hot soup.

specDecoder.meaning: A bell-shaped foot that reduces suction and splatter.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Braun uses it; the others use a plain guard.

specDecoder.meaning: A button that runs the motor at full speed while pressed.
specDecoder.watchFor: The KOIOS 5-in-1 and Bonsenkitchen include one.
KOIOS lists 304 on its shaft and blade.

howWeEvaluated.title: Blade and shaft design
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the foot geometry and guard. The Braun's bell shaft and KOIOS anti-scratch guard led. A bare blade scored lower.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power in context
howWeEvaluated.description: We read wattage as a loose guide because ratings are peak figures. The Braun at 350W and the Turelar at 1100W bracket the group. We did not rank by wattage alone.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed dial, trigger and two-speed layouts. The KOIOS 12-speed dial and Turelar trigger gave the finest control. The Braun and MasterChef are simpler.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit usefulness
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted the attachments that change what you can cook. The Bonsenkitchen processor and KOIOS chopper stood out. Unused extras earned no credit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value at the $50 cap
howWeEvaluated.description: Every item has a live listing price at or below the cap, ranked in relative tiers. We rely on spec sheets and owner feedback patterns, not our own blending. The Braun is the upper-middle tier and the MasterChef the third cheapest.

rows: Hot soups in a nonstick pot

cards.label: Dial
cards.text: The KOIOS models set a speed and hold it, which suits steady blending of a pot. The dial can be fiddly one-handed.

cards.label: Trigger
cards.text: The Turelar varies speed with finger pressure, giving instant control. It takes practice and tires the hand on long jobs.

howToChoose.note: Choose a dial for batch work and a trigger if you prefer feathering the speed.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A bell or guarded foot, a low speed to start and a stainless shaft that tolerates heat. Let the soup cool slightly before blending.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Braun's bell shaft is the best match, and the KOIOS 12-speed dial lets you start slowly.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You blend often and want better splatter control and a brand with parts, which points to the Braun. Moving beyond this cap buys a stronger motor and cordless options.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You blend a soup now and then. The MasterChef or KOIOS 3-in-1 cover that.

maintenance.why: Dried food in the bell or guard is hard to remove. Run the blender in warm soapy water for ten seconds.
Water in the motor housing is the usual failure. Wipe it with a damp cloth.
A cracked guard can let the blade scrape cookware. Replace it if damaged.
Boiling soup can spray. Let it sit for a minute and start at low speed.
Cord kinks near the handle can break the wire. Coil loosely and never wrap the cord tightly around the motor head, because the repeated bend at the strain relief is where most breaks start.

faq.a: Not necessarily. The headline numbers are peak ratings, and blade shape matters as much. The Braun at 350W handles soups well because of its bell shaft.

faq.q: What does $50 buy in an immersion blender?
faq.a: A corded stick, one or two speeds or variable control, and basic attachments. You do not get cordless or thick-batter power. Prices move, so the cap reflects listing prices at the time of the update.
Yes, in the pot, after letting it cool slightly. Start on low speed and keep the blade submerged to avoid splatter.

faq.q: Will it scratch my nonstick pot?
faq.a: A bare steel blade can. The KOIOS anti-scratch and Turelar nylon guards reduce the risk. Keep the blade off the pot floor.
Not reliably. Immersion blenders at this tier struggle with ice and frozen fruit. Use a countertop blender instead.
The motor can last years with careful use. Never submerge the housing, and clean the shaft right away.
